html:
The Omaha, Umoⁿhoⁿ in their own language, meaning "against the current", are a Siouan people of the Missouri River in northeast Nebraska. They speak a Dhegiha language close to those of the Ponca, Osage and Kaw, and their traditions say these peoples once lived together further east before moving west.

By the 1700s they lived in earth lodge villages on the Missouri, farming maize and going out on bison hunts twice a year. Their chief Blackbird made them a strong trading power, until smallpox in 1800 to 1801 killed many of them, Blackbird among them. In 1854 they gave up most of their land and kept a reservation at Macy, Nebraska.

The city of Omaha is named after them. The La Flesche family, including Susan La Flesche Picotte, the first Native American woman to become a doctor, became well known Omaha voices. See also Omaha.
